title: Swap Execution Facility Order Book Requirement for Permitted Transactions

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) proposes to amend 17 CFR 37.3(a)(2) to eliminate the requirement that Swap Execution Facilities (SEFs) offer an electronic order book for 'Permitted Transactions'—swaps that are not subject to the mandatory trade execution requirement under Section 2(h)(8) of the Commodity Exchange Act. The proposed rule seeks to codify CFTC Staff No-Action Letter 25-24, reasoning that mandatory order books for illiquid or episodically traded swaps impose heavy operational and financial costs on SEFs while generating negligible trading volume and minimal pre-trade price transparency.
ai_data.challenges: The proposal suffers from three major defects. First, legally and procedurally under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), the CFTC relies on isolated representations from select SEF operators rather than conducting a broad empirical evaluation of market-wide pre-trade transparency, thereby failing to demonstrate how a blanket removal aligns with its statutory mandate under CEA Section 5h(e) to promote pre-trade transparency. Second, economically, eliminating order books entirely without establishing a conditional or volume-based threshold mechanism risks locking in dealer-centric market fragmentation (e.g., RFQ-to-3 or voice execution), foreclosing opportunities for buy-side liquidity provision and wider quote competition as markets evolve. Third, the rule fails to consider hybrid transparency alternatives, such as mandatory indicative pricing streams or low-cost central limit order displays, which would preserve pre-trade price discovery without imposing full matching-engine overhead.

COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND MARKET STRUCTURE ANALYSTS

To: Christopher Kirkpatrick, Secretary
Commodity Futures Trading Commission
Three Lafayette Centre, 1155 21st Street NW, Washington, DC 20581

Re: Swap Execution Facility Order Book Requirement for Permitted Transactions (RIN 3038-AF79; 91 FR 55030, August 26, 2026)

I. INTRODUCTION AND EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's ('CFTC' or 'Commission') Notice of Proposed Rulemaking ('NPRM') regarding amendments to 17 CFR Part 37, 'Swap Execution Facility Order Book Requirement for Permitted Transactions' (91 FR 55030). 

While we recognize the operational costs highlighted by SEF operators on pages 55032–55033 of the NPRM, we strongly object to the complete, unconditioned elimination of the Order Book Requirement for all Permitted Transactions. CEA Section 5h(e) explicitly establishes that a primary statutory goal of SEFs is to promote pre-trade price transparency and trading on SEFs. A blanket removal of the minimum order book functionality for all non-mandated swaps—regardless of liquidity, trading volume, or product evolution—undermines these statutory directives and risks enshrining opaque, multi-dealer request-for-quote (RFQ) and voice workflows as permanent market fixtures.

II. SPECIFIC COMMENTS AND LEGAL DEFICIENCIES

1. APA Procedural and Empirical Deficiencies (91 FR 55032)
In Section II.A.1, the Commission bases its rationale primarily on NAL No. 25-24 and self-reported data from select registrants (e.g., LSEG SEF and Bloomberg SEF). Relying on qualitative assertions of operational burden without establishing a standardized, empirical evaluation across all registered SEFs creates an inadequate administrative record under 5 U.S.C. 706. The low usage of order books historically is partly a symptom of dealer preference for RFQ workflows rather than an inherent failure of order book mechanics.

2. Failure to Adopt a Volume-Based or Tiered Threshold (Response to Request for Comment #2, 91 FR 55033)
In Request for Comment #2 (p. 55033), the Commission asks whether it should use 'another method, such as trading volume in a certain swap, to require the use of an Order Book for some Permitted Transactions.' We strongly advocate for a volume-based threshold. Permitted Transactions are not a homogenous class; certain liquid benchmark swaps that have not yet been formally made subject to a trade execution requirement under Section 2(h)(8) possess sufficient activity to support order book price discovery. A dynamic threshold ensures that as a Permitted Transaction matures in volume and liquidity, market participants benefit from pre-trade order book transparency automatically.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT

To balance operational burdens against the statutory mandate to promote pre-trade transparency, we propose modifying 17 CFR 37.3(a)(2) to incorporate a conditional liquidity assessment standard rather than a total exemption:

Proposed Revision to § 37.3(a)(2):

'§ 37.3 Requirements and procedures for registration.
(a) * * *
(2) Minimum trading functionality. 
(i) Required Transactions. A swap execution facility shall, at a minimum, offer an Order Book as defined in paragraph (a)(3) of this section for Required Transactions as defined in § 37.9(a)(1).
(ii) Permitted Transactions. A swap execution facility shall offer an Order Book for Permitted Transactions, as defined in § 37.9(c)(1), that meet or exceed quarterly trading volume and liquidity thresholds established by the Commission. For all other Permitted Transactions, a swap execution facility may satisfy minimum trading functionality by offering an Order Book or an alternative trading functionality that displays executable or indicative quotes to all market participants on the facility.'

IV. CONCLUSION
The Commission should refine its proposal to ensure that market structure reform actively encourages competitive, pre-trade price transparency, rather than permanently deregulating execution methods for non-cleared or non-mandated swaps.

title: Pro Rata Share of Subpart F Income, Tested Income, or Tested Loss

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: This proposed regulation from the Internal Revenue Service and Department of the Treasury implements statutory amendments from the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) regarding how United States shareholders calculate their pro rata share of Subpart F income, tested income, and tested loss from Controlled Foreign Corporations (CFCs). It eliminates former rules requiring ownership on the 'last relevant day' and replaces them with a daily proration regime across periods of ownership during the CFC's taxable year. Additionally, the rule establishes mandatory taxable year closing upon a CFC status change event and provides a 50% ownership variance elective year-closing mechanism, while phasing out extraordinary reduction rules under §1.245A-5.
ai_data.challenges:
1. Administrative Procedure Act (APA) Arbitrary & Capricious Weakness: The rigid mandatory application of daily proration under proposed § 1.951-1(e)(2) without an interim closing of books or an 'extraordinary items' exception fails to account for major discrete income events (such as substantial asset dispositions) occurring before or after ownership transfers. Failing to provide standard accounting exceptions misallocates tax burdens contrary to economic reality and administrative precedents (e.g., Treas. Reg. § 1.706-4 and § 1.1502-76(b)).

2. Overly Restrictive Elective Year-Closing Threshold: Proposed § 1.951-1(d)(2) restricts elective year-closing exclusively to transactions resulting in a greater than 50 percentage point shift among non-related shareholders. For transfers between 10% and 50%, selling U.S. shareholders lose operational control yet remain fully exposed to post-closing actions of buyers that inflate Subpart F or GILTI inclusion amounts without contractual recourse or remedy.

3. Excessively Onerous Substantiation Requirements: Proposed § 1.951-4(h) rejects public comments on Notice 2025-75 and mandates onerous, subjective third-party documentation to prove a dividend increased taxable income for transition rule purposes. The refusal to provide a administrative safe harbor or per se rule creates severe compliance friction for historical, closed transactions.

RE: Comments on Proposed Regulations under Sections 951, 951A, and 6038 (REG-115646-25; RIN 1545-BR77): Pro Rata Share of Subpart F Income, Tested Income, or Tested Loss

Dear Officers and Drafting Counsel:

We submit these comments in response to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking published in the Federal Register (91 FR 55037-55062) on August 26, 2026. While we support Treasury and the IRS's efforts to implement the statutory revisions under the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), key aspects of the proposed regulations impose significant economic distortions and administrative burdens that fail the standards of reasoned decision-making under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

1. Need for an Extraordinary Items Exception in Daily Proration (§ 1.951-1(e)(2))
As drafted, proposed § 1.951-1(e)(2) mandates a pure daily proration approach for allocating a CFC's Subpart F income, tested income, and tested loss when ownership shifts during the year. This blanket method creates significant economic distortions if a CFC recognizes a large extraordinary gain (such as a discrete asset sale under Section 337 or Section 1001) either prior to or following a stock transfer. A taxpayer selling stock early in the year could be retroactively allocated a pro rata share of Subpart F income generated by an extraordinary transaction conducted months later by an unrelated buyer.

Recommendation: Treasury and the IRS should adopt an 'extraordinary items' exception modeled on Treas. Reg. § 1.706-4 and § 1.1502-76(b). Under this exception, extraordinary discrete gains or losses would be specifically allocated to the period in which they occurred rather than prorated daily across the entire taxable year.

2. Lowering the Threshold for Elective Closing of Taxable Year (§ 1.951-1(d)(2))
Proposed § 1.951-1(d)(2) limits the elective closing of a CFC's taxable year to cases where there is a 'significant ownership variance' exceeding 50 percentage points among non-related shareholders. This threshold is overly restrictive. A shareholder disposing of a 20% or 30% stake frequently surrenders operational oversight and lacks the audit rights or contractual power to prevent buyers from altering business operations or tax choices before year-end.

Recommendation: Lower the threshold for an elective year-closing under proposed § 1.951-1(d)(2)(ii)(A) from 50 percentage points to 20 percentage points, or permit a joint election whenever a U.S. shareholder disposes of its entire stock interest in a CFC.

3. Adoption of a Safe Harbor for Transition Rule Substantiation (§ 1.951-4(h))
Proposed § 1.951-4(h) mandates that taxpayers submit a detailed statement proving that a dividend increased a U.S. person's taxable income without establishing clear safe harbors for taxpayers who lack third-party access.

Recommendation: Adopt a per se safe harbor stating that dividends received by domestic corporations subject to standard federal corporate income tax (where no deduction under Section 245A or foreign tax credit offsets apply) automatically satisfy the substantiation requirement.

PROPOSED REGULATORY TEXT CHANGES:

Modify proposed § 1.951-1(d)(2)(ii)(A) as follows:
"(A) In general. A significant ownership variance occurs if, taking into account all specified transfers that occur pursuant to the same plan during the same taxable year of a controlled foreign corporation... the percentage of the outstanding stock of the controlled foreign corporation owned by one or more section 958(a) U.S. shareholders decreases, in the aggregate, by [REPLACE: more than 50 percentage points] [WITH: 20 percentage points or more, or results in a complete disposition of a section 958(a) U.S. shareholder's interest]."

Modify proposed § 1.951-1(e)(2)(i)(A) as follows:
"(A) Daily proration. Subject to paragraph (e)(2)(i)(B) of this section and paragraph (e)(2)(i)(C) (Extraordinary Items Exception), if the controlled foreign corporation has only one class of stock outstanding..."

Respectfully submitted,
[Civic Advocates & Policy Coalition]

COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND POLICY ANALYSTS ON THE PROPOSED RULE:
List of Approved Spent Fuel Storage Casks: TN Americas, LLC Standardized NUHOMS Horizontal Modular Storage System, Renewed Amendment No. 19
Docket ID: NRC-2026-2806 | RIN: 3150-AL72 | 10 CFR Part 72

I. INTRODUCTION & EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
We submit these public comments regarding the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's (NRC) proposed rule to approve Renewed Amendment No. 19 to Certificate of Compliance (CoC) No. 1004 for the TN Americas, LLC Standardized NUHOMS Horizontal Modular Storage System (88 FR 55028, August 26, 2026). While design optimizations that streamline manufacturing are understandable, the proposed implementation of a staggered plate design in the 61BTH basket introduces structural, thermal, and regulatory questions that require comprehensive public disclosure and technical justification prior to final approval.

II. SPECIFIC TECHNICAL AND LEGAL DEFECTS

1. Inadequate Structural and Thermal Margin Justification (88 FR 55028, Section I / Safety Evaluation Report ML26103A252):
The NRC proposes approving the 61BTH staggered plate basket based on technical similarities to the 24PTH Type 3 basket (CoC 1004, Amend 18) and EOS 37PTH/89BTH baskets (CoC 1042). However, changing the geometry of structural plates directly affects thermal dissipation capacity and load distribution during drop or seismic events. The rule relies heavily on design analogies rather than providing fully unredacted finite element dynamic impact modeling and transient heat transfer analyses for high-burnup fuel loads. Under 10 CFR 72.236(l), dry storage designs must evaluate structural integrity under normal, off-normal, and accident conditions; cross-referencing separate CoC approvals without providing integrated, public stress-strain evaluations for the modified 61BTH basket prevents meaningful public review under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 553.

2. Reliance on Outdated Environmental Assessments (88 FR 55030, Section VI):
The NRC cites environmental assessments dated 1989 (ML051230231) and 2010 (ML100710441) to satisfy its NEPA obligations. The physical properties of high-burnup fuel, combined with the extended storage periods envisioned under the CoC 1004 renewal, create thermal stress and cladding degradation risks that were not analyzed in 1989 or 2010. Reliance on legacy environmental documents to justify structural basket weight reductions for renewed CoCs fails to satisfy NEPA's mandate for a 'hard look' at cumulative environmental impacts.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE WORDING AND REGULATORY ACTION

To ensure complete safety and regulatory compliance, the NRC should withdraw the direct final rule and issue a revised proposed rule incorporating the following text within the 10 CFR 72.214 entry for CoC No. 1004, Renewed Amendment No. 19:

Proposed Technical Specification Requirement Addition:
"For the 61BTH improved basket design using staggered plates, general licensees shall verify that site-specific seismic acceleration limits and peak cladding temperature margins do not exceed the baseline parameters established in Revision 0 of the Safety Evaluation Report. Prior to first use of the 61BTH staggered plate configuration for spent fuel exceeding 45,000 MWd/MTU burnup, licensees must conduct a finite element structural dynamic analysis confirming basket plate integrity under maximum credible drop and seismic scenarios, and submit the analysis to the NRC for public docketing under Docket ID NRC-2026-2806."

IV. CONCLUSION
The NRC must ensure that economic and manufacturing convenience does not compromise structural redundancy or environmental review standards. We urge the Commission to address these comments as significant adverse comments under the procedure described at 88 FR 55029, withdraw the direct final rule, and publish a detailed supplemental evaluation for public review.

title: Membership Adjustment of the Mushroom Council

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The USDA Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS) proposes to amend the Mushroom Promotion, Research, and Consumer Information Order (7 CFR Part 1209) by realigning the geographic regions and member seats on the Mushroom Council. Specifically, the rule reallocates one Council seat from Region 1 (Eastern/Other States) to Region 3 (Western States) based on 4-year average production and shipment data. Reliance on Unvalidated Proxy Data: Because USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) discontinued individual state-level reporting for California in 2025, AMS estimated production ratios for Regions 1 and 3 using static 2022 Census of Agriculture square-footage figures. Applying 2022 square-footage proportions to 2021-2024 NASS production data assumes constant yield per square foot across all regions and time periods. This methodology is scientifically flawed, fails to reflect regional efficiency gains, and introduces arbitrary estimates into formal rulemaking.

Severe Governance Disproportion for Importers: Importers contribute roughly 198 million pounds annually (~22-30% of total U.S. mushroom volume), yet remain capped at 1 member out of 9 (11% representation). While statutory limits exist, AMS relies on a rigid reallocation framework without providing economic analysis on the disparate assessment-to-representation ratio imposed on importers.

3. Procedural Shortcomings and Inadequate Comment Period: A truncated 30-day comment window limits the ability of small producers in Region 1—who stand to lose 33% of their voting power—to conduct independent data collection to verify or challenge AMS's square-footage allocation estimates.

Re: Comments on Proposed Rule: Membership Adjustment of the Mushroom Council; 7 CFR Part 1209; Docket No. AMS-SC-25-0551; 91 FR 54814 (August 25, 2026).

I. INTRODUCTION & SUMMARY
These comments are submitted regarding the Agricultural Marketing Service's (AMS) proposed rule to reallocate seats on the Mushroom Council from Region 1 to Region 3. While periodic reapportionment is authorized under 7 U.S.C. 6104 and 7 CFR 1209.30, the methodology employed by AMS to derive regional volume figures relies on unvalidated proxy estimates that violate core principles of administrative reasoned decision-making under the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. 706).

II. PROCEDURAL AND EMPIRICAL DEFECTS IN DATA ESTIMATION (91 FR 54815-54816)
On pages 54815 and 54816, AMS acknowledges that NASS ceased publishing individual state production data for California in 2025. To compensate, AMS calculated a fixed ratio (45% for Region 1 and 55% for Region 3) using growing area square footage from the 2022 Census of Agriculture, and applied this 2022 static ratio across all 2021–2024 production figures.

This proxy methodology is fundamentally flawed:
1. Yield Variability: Crop yield per square foot differs significantly between advanced commercial growing operations in California/West and legacy operations in the East. Assuming uniform productivity across all square footage introduces systemic bias.
2. Temporal Mismatch: A static 2022 area metric cannot accurately capture dynamic shifts in production efficiency or farm closures occurring in 2023 and 2024.
3. Lack of Empirical Validation: AMS failed to cross-validate these proxy calculations against actual assessment collection records held by the Mushroom Council.

III. SMALL BUSINESS AND RFA IMPACTS (91 FR 54816)
Under the Initial Regulatory Flexibility Act Analysis, AMS notes that 96% of mushroom producers (1,213 of 1,258) are small entities. Removing a seat from Region 1 dilutes the representation of small, independent growers in the Eastern U.S. who rely on Council activities for regional research and promotion, without providing a verified empirical basis for the reduction.

IV. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE ACTION AND REGULATORY TEXT

Under ICR, twin-engine transport helicopters can operate one engine at low stand-by idle while the active engine provides 100% of required cruise power to significantly improve fuel efficiency and extend flight range. The proposed special conditions create new definitions, operating limitations, control system requirements, and modified testing criteria for icing, rain ingestion, endurance, and transient power response under 14 CFR Part 33.
ai_data.challenges:
The primary challenges and regulatory defects in the proposed special conditions concern safety margins during sudden engine-out emergencies, environmental icing risk, thermal fatigue, and Administrative Procedure Act (APA) procedural sufficiency:

1. Safety and Acceleration Response Latency (§ 33.73): Allowing up to 5 seconds for an engine to transition from ICR stand-by power to 95% takeoff power creates a critical performance lag. In the event of a sudden flameout or failure of the active engine, a 5-second recovery delay risks significant rotor droop, control loss, or rapid loss of altitude before the stand-by engine can supply sufficient power.
2. Environmental Icing and Relight Risk (§ 33.68 & § 33.78): Because an engine operating at ICR stand-by produces substantially less waste heat, ice and water accumulation on intake blades, guide vanes, and combustor probes during extended low-power cruise in icing or heavy rain conditions could cause engine flameout or delayed relight during sudden acceleration.
3. Thermal Shock and Low-Cycle Fatigue (§ 33.87): Rapidly cycling between low stand-by idle and maximum continuous or 2-minute emergency power subjects hot-section turbine components to severe thermal gradients and mechanical strain. The proposed endurance test cycles may fail to capture long-term low-cycle fatigue (LCF) and thermal mechanical fatigue (TMF) blade degradation over the engine's lifecycle.
4. Procedural & Substantiation Deficiencies under the APA: The FAA has not provided empirical test data or rotorcraft flight dynamics modeling to justify why a 5-second acceleration response time ensures an equivalent level of safety for transport category twin-engine helicopters operating under 14 CFR Part 29.

COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND SAFETY RESEARCHERS ON PROPOSED SPECIAL CONDITIONS

Docket No. FAA-2026-3073; Notice No. 33-25-03-SC
Special Conditions: Pratt and Whitney Canada, PW220A; New Engine Rating: Idle-Cruise Regime

I. INTRODUCTION AND EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
We submit these comments in response to the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Notice of Proposed Special Conditions for the Pratt & Whitney Canada (P&WC) Model PW220A engine. While we support fuel-efficiency innovations in rotorcraft propulsion, the proposed Idle-Cruise Regime (ICR) creates novel failure modes that demand stricter safety parameters to protect civil aviation safety under 14 CFR Part 33 and Part 29.

II. SPECIFIC TECHNICAL CONCERNS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Transient Acceleration Time Limits (§ 33.73 - Power or Thrust Response)
- Issue: The FAA proposes allowing a 5-second response time from rated ICR stand-by power to 95% rated takeoff power. In a twin-engine rotorcraft, if the active engine suffers an abrupt uncommanded shutdown during cruise, a 5-second delay before the stand-by engine reaches power will result in dangerous main rotor RPM decay (rotor droop).
- Recommendation: The acceleration time from ICR stand-by to 95% rated takeoff power must be shortened to no more than 3.0 seconds under all ambient temperatures and bleed air load conditions. Alternatively, the FAA must require an integrated automated rotorcraft flight control system override that prevents transient rotor droop beyond allowable safety limits.

2. Extended Icing Exposure and Ingestion Safety (§ 33.68 & § 33.78)
- Issue: Low engine thermal output during extended ICR stand-by flight in icing conditions increases the risk of ice accretion in the induction system and combustor flameout during rapid power expansion.
- Recommendation: Section 33.68 testing should require a minimum continuous 30-minute exposure at rated ICR stand-by power in continuous maximum icing conditions prior to rapid acceleration, ensuring no ice shed induces engine stall or flameout.

3. Endurance and Thermal Mechanical Fatigue Verification (§ 33.87)
- Issue: The proposed endurance cycles do not adequately account for the cumulative thermal mechanical fatigue (TMF) resulting from repeated rapid step-changes between cold stand-by idle and hot 2-minute ICR power.
- Recommendation: Add a mandatory supplemental low-cycle thermal shock test requiring 500 direct rapid acceleration/deceleration cycles between ICR stand-by and ICR 2-minute power to evaluate turbine blade erosion and creep failure modes.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT

We propose the following amendments to the proposed special condition text:

Section 33.73 Power or Thrust Response:
"The design and construction of the engine must enable an increase from the rated ICR stand-by power lever position to 95 percent rated takeoff power in not over 3.0 seconds. The 3.0-second power response must occur from a stabilized static condition using maximum allowable bleed air and accessories loads necessary to run the engine and rotorcraft services."

Section 33.68 Induction System Icing:
"Compliance with § 33.68 must be demonstrated at 'rated ICR stand-by power rotor speeds' for a continuous duration of not less than 30 minutes in standard icing conditions prior to demonstrating rapid engine acceleration without engine surge, stall, or flameout."

IV. CONCLUSION
The FAA should revise these special conditions to incorporate these essential safeguards prior to final issuance.

Re: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking – Fee for Certain H-1B Petitions (91 FR 54817-54839)

I. INTRODUCTION & STATEMENT OF INTEREST
The undersigned organization submits this public comment in response to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) titled "Fee for Certain H-1B Petitions," published at 91 FR 54817 (August 25, 2026). The proposed rule would establish an unprecedented $103,265 supplemental fee on all H-1B cap-subject petitions, creating an unsustainable burden on employers, higher education institutions, and small businesses.

II. STATUTORY DEFECTS: DHS EXCEEDS ITS AUTHORITY UNDER INA § 286(m) & (n)
As stated at 91 FR 54819–54820, DHS relies on Sections 286(m) and (n) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. § 1356(m) and (n), to justify recovering $8.8 billion across six federal agencies. However, Section 286(m) explicitly mandates that fee levels must ensure recovery of the full costs of "providing adjudication and naturalization services." 

Funding DOJ Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) court proceedings ($2.95 billion, 91 FR 54830), DOS Bureau of Population, Refugees, and Migration (PRM) overseas refugee travel ($66 million, 91 FR 54830), and CBP border technology ($76.2 million, 91 FR 54829) exceeds the statutory scope of "adjudication services." Under Supreme Court precedent in National Cable Television Ass'n v. United States, 415 U.S. 336 (1974), an administrative user fee that funds broad public benefits rather than specific services rendered to the payor constitutes an unconstitutional tax. DHS lacks statutory authority to levy an enterprise-wide immigration tax on H-1B employers.

III. ARBITRARY AND CAPRICIOUS COST SHIFTING UNDER THE APA
DHS concedes in the preamble (91 FR 54821) that it "has never directly transferred the costs of one program to another based on a determination that requestors under one program can afford higher fees more than other general or specific requestors." Suddenly abandoning established Activity-Based Costing (ABC) principles—which match fee levels with actual processing burdens—in favor of a subjective "ability-to-pay" standard violates 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A).

Furthermore, DHS relies on an unvetted working paper (Borjas 2026, 91 FR 54835) to assert that H-1B petition demand will remain at 85,000 despite a 2,000%+ fee increase. DHS failed to model the economic displacement of domestic innovation, talent migration to foreign jurisdictions, and downstream employer bankruptcy, rendering the rule's economic analysis fundamentally flawed.

In the Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) at 91 FR 54837, DHS admits that the proposed fee will have a "significant economic impact on 11,051 small entities (76 percent of small entities that filed cap-subject petitions)." Despite this severe finding, DHS summarily rejected small entity exemptions or fee reductions based on unsupported assertions regarding "perverse incentives." This failure to consider viable regulatory alternatives violates 5 U.S.C. § 603.

V. PROPOSED REGULATORY ALTERNATIVE Wording
To remedy these legal and procedural defects, DHS must withdraw the proposed 8 CFR § 106.2(a)(3)(xii) in its entirety. If DHS seeks to adjust H-1B filing fees, it must do so strictly based on USCIS's actual adjudication costs under established Activity-Based Costing methodologies.

Option A (Withdrawal):
"8 CFR 106.2(a)(3)(xii) [Removed and Reserved]"

Option B (Capped Adjudication Cost Alternative):
"8 CFR 106.2(a)(3)(xii): In addition to the fee prescribed in paragraph (a)(3)(i) of this section, an additional adjudication cost recovery fee for H-1B cap-subject petitions may be required in an amount not to exceed $1,200, representing solely the direct and indirect costs incurred by USCIS in adjudicating Form I-129 H-1B cap-subject petitions under section 286(m) of the Act."

Rationale: Proposed § 1523.1(c) states that 'a person that, for compensation or profit, engages in the business in the United States of issuing payment stablecoins is a digital asset service provider.' This interpretation conflates two distinct statutory roles created by Congress in Sections 2(7) and 2(23) of the Act. Forcing issuers into the DASP framework creates redundant regulatory obligations and subjects issuers to conflicting offer/sale restrictions intended solely for secondary intermediaries. Under Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 144 S. Ct. 2244 (2024), courts will not defer to Treasury's overbroad reading of clear statutory definitions.
Proposed Wording for § 1523.1(c):
"Digital asset service provider has the meaning set forth in section 2(7) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5901(7)). For the avoidance of doubt, an entity acting strictly in its capacity as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer or registered foreign payment stablecoin issuer under section 18(a) of the Act shall not be deemed a digital asset service provider solely by virtue of issuing or redeeming payment stablecoins in accordance with its statutory authority."

2. Due Process Deficiencies and Scienter Standard in Participation Penalties (§ 1523.2(d), 91 FR 53378, 53390)
Rationale: Proposed § 1523.2(d) enumerates examples of secondary activities—such as white-label branding, software coordination, or market making—that constitute criminal 'participation' under Section 3(f) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5902(f)). As drafted, this section lacks an explicit mens rea requirement, threatening market makers and software providers with strict criminal liability for routine liquidity activities. To satisfy Due Process and avoid impermissible vagueness, Treasury must clarify that criminal participation requires actual knowledge and intentional facilitation of an unlawful issuance.
Proposed Wording for § 1523.2(d):
"(d) A person knowingly participates in a violation of paragraph (a) for purposes of the penalty in section 3(f) of the Act (12 U.S.C. 5902(f)) only if the person has actual knowledge that the payment stablecoin issuance violates paragraph (a) and intentionally acts to facilitate such unlawful issuance by:
(1) Directly incurring a primary or secondary legal obligation to convert, redeem, or repurchase the unlawful payment stablecoin;
(2) Purposefully coordinating with the issuer to directly execute the unlawful minting or distribution; or
(3) Acting as a primary underwriter or designated market maker directly for the issuer in the initial distribution of the unlawfully issued payment stablecoin with actual knowledge of its unapproved status."

3. Adoption of a Bright-Line Regulation S Offshore Framework for DASPs (§ 1523.3(e), 91 FR 53384, 53390)
Rationale: The proposed due diligence standard in § 1523.3(c) and (e) creates an impossible verification burden for DASPs regarding foreign issuer code capabilities and future legal compliance. Treasury specifically requested comment on whether to adopt a Regulation S-style framework (Questions 45, 65). Adopting an offshore-transaction standard provides clarity, aligns with existing SEC compliance infrastructure, and prevents regulatory flowback issues without stifling domestic commerce.
Proposed Wording for § 1523.3(e):
"(e) Safe Harbor for Offshore Transactions. A digital asset service provider shall be deemed not to offer, sell, or make available a payment stablecoin to a person located in the United States if:
(1) The offer or sale is executed in an offshore transaction where the buyer is reasonably believed to be outside the United States at the time the order is placed;
(2) The digital asset service provider maintains IP-geofencing, identity verification, or contractual prohibitions reasonably designed to prevent access by U.S. residents; and
(3) The digital asset service provider does not engage in directed selling efforts or targeted marketing campaigns directed to individuals located in the United States."

III. CONCLUSION
Treasury should revise the proposed rule to respect statutory boundaries, provide explicit mens rea protections for secondary market actors, and implement a pragmatic Regulation S safe harbor.

I. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF INTEREST
We respectfully submit these comments in response to the Coast Guard’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) published at 91 FR 53395 (August 18, 2026), regarding the proposed 48-hour time limit for Bolivar Anchorage Area (A) East under 33 CFR 110.197(b)(2). While we support the Coast Guard's objective of enhancing port safety and managing navigation congestion, the proposed rule as written contains critical procedural defects under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and poses unstudied operational and economic risks to commercial maritime operations.

II. SPECIFIC COMMENTS AND LEGAL DEFECTS

1. Lack of Empirical Supporting Evidence in the Public Docket (91 FR 53395, Section II)
The preamble states that the Coast Guard determined the necessity of a 48-hour restriction '[a]fter discussion with the local maritime community during a Harbor Safety Committee meeting.' However, the Coast Guard has placed no empirical traffic studies, queuing data, or safety audit records into Docket No. USCG-2024-0667. Under the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), agency action is arbitrary and capricious if it relies on factors Congress did not intend, entirely fails to consider an important aspect of the problem, or offers an explanation that runs counter to the evidence. Informal committee dialogue alone does not constitute a robust factual basis for federal regulatory action.

2. Improper Regulatory Flexibility Certification (91 FR 53395-53396, Section IV.A)
The Coast Guard certifies under 5 U.S.C. § 605(b) that this rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities because it 'merely institutes a 48-hour time limitation in an already existing anchorage area.' This conclusion fails to consider the real-world operational realities of lightering, bunkering, and terminal delays in the Galveston/Houston ship channel. Forcing small vessel operators, tug/barge fleets, and ocean carriers to heave anchor after 48 hours to seek permissions or move offshore incurs hundreds of thousands of dollars annually in pilotage fees, fuel burn, and demurrage costs. A formal Regulatory Flexibility Analysis under 5 U.S.C. § 603 is required.

3. Operational Need for Lightering and Weather Exceptions (33 CFR 110.197(b)(2))
While the rule provides an exception for 'stress of weather,' it fails to explicitly accommodate ongoing commercial operations, such as ship-to-ship transfers (lightering), bunkering, or documented delays in berth availability at local facilities. Requiring vessels mid-transfer or awaiting berth clearances to submit individualized permission requests to the Captain of the Port (COPT) creates unnecessary administrative overhead for both the Coast Guard VTS and mariners.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE REGULATORY TEXT

To resolve these legal and operational deficiencies, we propose amending the regulatory text at 33 CFR 110.197(b)(2) to explicitly incorporate operational extensions for ongoing cargo operations, bunkering, and terminal congestion delays:

Proposed Revision to 33 CFR § 110.197(b)(2):

"(2) Except when stress of weather makes sailing impractical or hazardous, or when engaged in active lightering, bunkering, or awaiting documented terminal berth availability, vessels shall not anchor in anchorage areas (A), (A) East, (B), or (C) for more than 48 hours unless expressly authorized by the Captain of the Port Houston-Galveston. Permission to anchor for longer periods may be requested through Coast Guard Vessel Traffic Service Houston/Galveston on VHF-FM channels 12 (156.60 MHz) or 13 (156.65 MHz) or via electronic notification. An extension of up to 48 additional hours shall be routinely granted for vessels demonstrating active lightering or pending terminal readiness."

IV. CONCLUSION
We urge the Coast Guard to perform a complete economic impact analysis and revise 33 CFR 110.197(b)(2) with flexible operational language prior to issuing a Final Rule.

The proposed rule fails to satisfy the basic notice requirements of Section 553 of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 553, due to fatal factual, mathematical, and nomenclature errors:

Critical Longitude Discrepancy: On page 53394, the FAA states that the Class E airspace boundary split line is 'centered approximately 250 feet west of the airport reference point' at long. 151°50'13" W. 2. Conflicting Facility Naming: Page 53394 refers to the facility as 'Trader Bay Production Airport' in 'The Proposal' narrative, whereas the title, summary, and legal designation use 'Trading Bay Production Airport'. 

Because the public cannot determine the true legal boundaries of the proposed airspace from this flawed notice, the FAA must issue a corrected Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (SNPRM).

III. UNADRESSED IMPACTS ON VFR GENERAL AVIATION AND AIR TAXI OPERATIONS
The Cook Inlet coastal corridor is a vital low-altitude transit route for Visual Flight Rules (VFR) general aviation pilots, commercial air charter services, and local fishery support flights. Establishing Class E airspace down to 700 feet AGL imposes 14 CFR § 91.155 VFR weather minimums (3 miles visibility, 500 ft below / 1,000 ft above clouds), depriving pilots of the Class G daylight weather minimums (1 mile visibility, clear of clouds). In Alaska’s frequent ceiling and visibility constrained climate, this action creates a critical low-altitude bottleneck, forcing unequipped VFR aircraft into hazardous terrain or offshore maritime routes.

I. INTRODUCTION AND OVERVIEW
These comments are submitted in response to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and Department of the Treasury's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking published in the Federal Register at 91 FR 53217 (August 17, 2026). We support the Treasury Department's deregulatory initiative to reduce unnecessary reporting obligations for trusts. II. SPECIFIC COMMENTS AND LEGAL ANALYSIS

1. Administrative Cliff Effect of the 'Solely' Requirement (91 FR 53219 / Proposed § 1.6034-1(b)(3))
As drafted, proposed 26 CFR § 1.6034-1(b)(3) exempts a trust from filing Form 1041-A only if its 'only claimed deductions under section 642(c) of the Code are attributable to contributions taken into account... under section 702(a)(4)... or section 1366(a)(1)'. 
This creates an impractical 'cliff effect.' If a trust earns $1,000,000 in passthrough charitable deductions via Schedule K-1 and makes a minor direct cash donation of $100 to a local community foundation, the trust forfeits the exception entirely and must file a comprehensive Form 1041-A. To fulfill the agency's stated goal of administrative burden reduction, Treasury should implement a de minimis safe harbor for direct contributions or allow proportional reporting relief.

2. Clarification for Multi-Tiered Passthrough Structures (91 FR 53219 / Proposed § 1.6034-1(b)(3))
Modern wealth management frequently utilizes tiered entities (e.g., a trust owning an interest in an upper-tier holding LLC, which owns a operating partnership). While the preamble notes that indirect ownership is covered, the regulatory text in § 1.6034-1(b)(3) references deductions taken into account under section 702(a)(4) or 1366(a)(1) without explicitly referencing multi-tiered passthrough chains. The regulatory text should explicitly clarify that indirect flow-through contributions through multiple tiers of partnerships or S corporations fall within the exception.

3. Statutory Authority and APA Considerations (91 FR 53218 / 26 U.S.C. § 6034)
IRC § 6034(b)(2) explicitly details statutory exceptions enacted by Congress to the general reporting rule of § 6034(b)(1). Under modern administrative law principles (see Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 144 S. Ct. 2244 (2024)), Treasury must ensure its regulatory exceptions strictly align with statutory delegations. To reinforce the legal durability of this rule under the Administrative Procedure Act, Treasury should explicitly ground this regulatory exception in its general authority under IRC § 7805(a) to define terms and prescribe necessary rules for forms and returns under IRC § 6034(b)(1).

III. PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO REGULATORY TEXT

We propose the following revisions to 26 CFR § 1.6034-1:

1. Amend § 1.6034-1(b)(3) to read as follows:

'(3) Trusts claiming section 642(c) deductions resulting from amounts paid by a passthrough entity. 
(i) In general. A trust is not required to file a Form 1041-A (or a successor form) for a taxable year if the trust's claimed deductions under section 642(c) of the Code for such year are attributable directly or indirectly to contributions taken into account by the trust under section 702(a)(4) of the Code, section 1366(a)(1) of the Code, or both, including through multi-tiered passthrough entities.
(ii) De minimis exception for direct contributions. A trust shall also be eligible for the exception in paragraph (b)(3)(i) of this section if the trust's direct charitable contributions claiming a deduction under section 642(c) do not exceed the lesser of $5,000 or 5 percent of the total deduction claimed under section 642(c) for the taxable year.'

IV. CONCLUSION
We urge the IRS and Treasury to adopt these amendments to eliminate administrative cliff effects, provide certainty for tiered holding structures, and strengthen the legal foundation of the final regulations.

title: Gastroenterology-Urology Devices; Reclassification of Diagnostic Endoscopic Light Source Systems To Be Renamed Cystoscopic Systems Intended as an Aid for Detection of Bladder Cancer

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is proposing to reclassify diagnostic endoscopic light source systems intended as an aid for bladder cancer detection (product code OAY) from class III (PMA) to class II (special controls) subject to 510(k) premarket notification. The proposed rule creates a new classification regulation under 21 CFR 876.1560 titled 'Cystoscopic system intended as an aid for detection of bladder cancer' and outlines specific special controls for clinical data, optical performance, software, reprocessing, and labeling. This action aims to lower administrative burdens, foster market competition, and accelerate patient access to adjunctive blue-light cystoscopy technologies.
ai_data.challenges: The primary legal defect in the proposed order is the blanket requirement under proposed 21 CFR 876.1560(b)(1) mandating clinical data for all subsequent 510(k) premarket notifications. This creates a high evidentiary threshold that mimics class III PMA requirements and conflicts with the 'least burdensome' mandate established in Section 513(a)(3)(D) of the FD&C Act and 21 U.S.C. 360c(c). Scientifically, the special controls fail to provide objective, standardized optical benchmarking metrics (e.g., exact tolerance thresholds for wavelength bandwidths, excitation filter power density, and camera sensor gain), which risks high variability in diagnostic sensitivity across different device manufacturers. Economically, tying device clearance strictly to specific cross-labeled drugs without clear interoperability protocols creates a proprietary bottleneck, locking healthcare providers into single-source drug-device combinations and limiting competitive entry.

COMMENTS OF CIVIC ADVOCATES AND POLICY ANALYSTS

Docket No. FDA-2026-N-8249
Reclassification of Diagnostic Endoscopic Light Source Systems To Be Renamed Cystoscopic Systems Intended as an Aid for Detection of Bladder Cancer (21 CFR Part 876)

I. Executive Summary
We applaud the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for proposing to reclassify diagnostic endoscopic light source systems (product code OAY) from Class III (premarket approval) to Class II (special controls). Reclassification will facilitate broader clinical availability of blue-light cystoscopy. However, key aspects of the proposed special controls under 21 CFR 876.1560 impose unnecessary regulatory burdens and lack clear scientific standardization.

II. Statutory and Legal Defects: Violation of the Least Burdensome Mandate
Proposed 21 CFR 876.1560(b)(1) states that 'Clinical data must confirm accurate detection of bladder cancer when used with the approved optical imaging agent(s).' Mandating clinical data for every 510(k) submission, regardless of whether a device demonstrates optical and technological equivalence to a predicate, violates Section 513(a)(3)(D) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 360c(a)(3)(D)), which directs FDA to utilize the least burdensome means of establishing substantial equivalence.

III. Scientific and Labeling Concerns: False Positives and Optical Standardization
Photodynamic blue-light cystoscopy inherently carries a risk of false positives, particularly in patients with recent intravesical therapy (such as BCG) or active tissue inflammation (see Ray et al., 2010). The proposed special controls lack required warnings regarding confounding mucosal conditions and fail to define specific technical thresholds for optical spectral bandwidths and filter tolerances.

IV. Proposed Regulatory Text Revisions
We respectfully request that FDA amend proposed 21 CFR 876.1560(b) as follows:

1. Modify paragraph (b)(1) to permit bench performance testing in lieu of clinical trials when technological equivalence is demonstrated:
   '(b)(1) Clinical data, or non-clinical optical bench performance testing demonstrating equivalent excitation and emission spectral profiles, must confirm accurate detection of bladder cancer when used with the compatible approved optical imaging agent(s)...'

2. Amend paragraph (b)(9)(iv) to require explicit clinical warnings:
   '(b)(9)(iv) A warning that the device should not be used as the only or definitive basis for diagnosis, alongside specific clinical warnings detailing the risk of false-positive fluorescence in patients with concurrent mucosal inflammation or recent intravesical therapy (e.g., BCG administration within 90 days).'

title: Medical Devices; Classification of Accessories Distinct From Other Devices; Proposed List of Accessories Suitable for Class I; Request for Comments

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is issuing a proposed rule pursuant to Section 707 of the FDA Reauthorization Act of 2017 (FDARA) to distinctly classify seven specific medical device accessories into Class I, exempting them from premarket notification (510(k)) requirements. The Agency asserts that general controls alone provide reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness for these accessories, independent of the higher-risk classifications assigned to their parent devices. The proposed accessories span cardiovascular, gastroenterology-urology, and general surgical device categories.
ai_data.challenges: The proposed rule presents critical legal, scientific, and regulatory flaws under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA, 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A)) and the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act). First, distinct classification into Class I automatically exempts non-software devices from mandatory Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR) design controls under 21 CFR 820.10(c)(2). Removing both 510(k) premarket oversight and design controls for accessories used in high-stakes environments—such as ECMO mounting/priming equipment (870.4100), implantable pacemaker ECG cables (870.3610), and defibrillator battery chargers (870.5300)—creates unmitigated risks of electrical interference, battery overheating, mechanical failure, or circuit detachment. Second, FDA's assertion that general controls alone are sufficient lacks empirical risk assessment and fails to establish clear compatibility or material standards, rendering the proposed reclassification arbitrary and capricious.

ai_data.proposed_comment:
PUBLIC COMMENT ON PROPOSED RULE

Agency: Food and Drug Administration (FDA), HHS
Docket No.: FDA-2025-N-6224
Title: Medical Devices; Classification of Accessories Distinct From Other Devices; Proposed List of Accessories Suitable for Class I; Request for Comments
Federal Register Citation: 91 FR 53205–53209 (August 17, 2026)

I. INTRODUCTORY STATEMENT AND INTEREST OF COMMENTER
This public comment is submitted in response to the Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) proposed list of medical device accessories for distinct classification into Class I under Section 513(f)(6)(D)(i) of the FD&C Act, as amended by FDARA. While we support statutory efforts to reduce administrative burdens where risks are genuinely low, we write to express serious concerns regarding the deregluation of accessories connected to critical care and life-sustaining equipment.

II. LEGAL AND TECHNICAL DEFICIENCIES

1. Inadequate Consideration of Design Control Exemptions (820.10(c) / Page 53207)
On page 53207, column 1, FDA notes that design and development controls generally do not apply to Class I devices unless automated with computer software or listed in 21 CFR 820.10(c)(2). By placing accessories such as ECMO accessories (870.4100) and defibrillator chargers (870.5300) into Class I without explicitly subjecting them to design controls under 820.10(c)(2), FDA creates a significant regulatory vacuum. Without design controls, manufacturers are not legally required to validate physical compatibility, thermal management, or structural integrity, raising severe patient safety issues.

2. Unreasonable Risk of Harm for Critical-Care Accessories (Table 1, Page 53208)
- Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO) Accessories (21 CFR 870.4100 / QJZ, QNR): Priming equipment and mounting brackets directly impact mechanical stability in life-sustaining extracorporeal circuits. A bracket failure or priming leak during patient transport or bedside care can result in catastrophic decannulation or blood line interruption.
- Pacemaker ECG Cable Accessories (21 CFR 870.3610 / DXY, OSR): Signal noise, electromagnetic incompatibility, or mechanical pin slippage in pacemaker cables directly distorts pacing diagnostics and cardiac monitoring.
- Auxiliary Power Supplies for Defibrillators (21 CFR 870.5300 / MPD): Defibrillator battery chargers must maintain strict voltage tolerances to ensure emergency resuscitation availability and prevent thermal runaway.

3. Administrative Procedure Act Violation (5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A))
FDA's proposal fails to provide empirical safety data demonstrating that general controls alone are sufficient to mitigate mechanical and electrical interface failures for these specific product codes. Proceeding without such a basis renders the classification arbitrary, capricious, and unsupported by substantial evidence.

III. PROPOSED REGULATORY ALTERNATIVES AND TEXT AMENDMENTS

We respectfully request that FDA adopt the following modifications in its final action:

1. Retain 510(k) Premarket Notification or Class II Status for Critical-Care Accessories:
Remove product codes QJZ, QNR (ECMO accessories), DXY, OSR (pacemaker cables), and MPD (defibrillator power supplies) from the final Class I distinct classification list.

2. Mandatory Design Control Condition under 21 CFR 820.10(c)(2):
If FDA proceeds with Class I reclassification for any accessory interfacing with critical or life-sustaining parent systems, FDA must amend 21 CFR 820.10(c)(2) to explicitly require QMSR Design Controls for those product codes.

3. Proposed Revision to Section III Text (Page 53207):
Amend Section III to read:
'FDA considers an accessory to be eligible for classification into class I distinct from another device if the accessory: (1) is not for use in supporting or sustaining human life, or of substantial importance in preventing impairment to human health; (2) does not present a potential unreasonable risk of illness or injury; (3) general controls alone would be sufficient to provide a reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness; AND (4) the accessory does not rely on critical physical, electrical, or signal-compatibility specifications with a life-supporting or life-sustaining parent system.'

title: Airspace Designations and Reporting Points: Santa Elena, TX

ai_data.summary_of_main_idea: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) proposes to amend 14 CFR Part 71 by revoking the Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface at Diamond 'O' Ranch Airport in Santa Elena, TX. This action follows the decommissioning of the Santa Elena radio beacon (RBN) and the formal cancellation of associated ground-based instrument procedures. The FAA asserts that controlled airspace is no longer necessary at this location because Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) operations are no longer supported.
ai_data.challenges: The primary legal and procedural challenge under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. 706(2)(A), is that the FAA failed to consider whether performance-based navigation—specifically RNAV (GPS) instrument approach procedures—should replace the decommissioned ground-based NDB/RBN before completely revoking the Class E airspace. Additionally, the agency relies on a cursory certification under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) that economic impacts are de minimis without gathering data on rural medical evacuation (medevac), emergency services, or agricultural aviation operations that may rely on low-altitude controlled transition airspace in remote South Texas.

RE: Docket No. FAA-2026-9901; Airspace Docket No. 26-ASW-13 – Notice of Proposed Rulemaking: Revocation of Class E Airspace; Santa Elena, TX (91 FR 53203-53204)

I. INTRODUCTION & SUMMARY
The undersigned submits these comments in response to the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) published at 91 FR 53203 on August 17, 2026, regarding the proposed revocation of Class E airspace at Diamond "O" Ranch Airport, Santa Elena, TX. While recognizing the agency's effort to decommission legacy non-directional radio beacons (RBN/NDB) under the NextGen transition, the complete revocation of Class E airspace without evaluating GPS/RNAV replacement procedures creates safety and operational risks for general aviation, emergency medical services, and agricultural operators in rural South Texas.

II. LEGAL AND PROCEDURAL DEFECTS UNDER THE APA AND RFA
1. Arbitrary & Capricious Failure to Consider RNAV Alternatives:
Under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), agency action is arbitrary and capricious if the agency fails to consider an important aspect of the problem. Section 40103 of Title 49 charges the FAA with ensuring the safety and efficient use of airspace. The FAA’s proposal (91 FR 53203) cites the cancellation of legacy instrument procedures and the decommissioning of the Santa Elena RBN as sole justification for revoking Class E airspace. However, the docket contains no study or analysis evaluating whether Area Navigation (RNAV/GPS) instrument approaches could or should be implemented at Diamond "O" Ranch Airport to preserve safe IFR access during adverse meteorological conditions.

2. Inadequate Small Entity and Safety Impact Analysis:
In the Regulatory Notices and Analyses section (91 FR 53204), the FAA certifies that the proposal will result in "de minimis costs" and will not have a significant economic impact on small entities. This finding lacks empirical support. Revoking controlled Class E airspace increases cloud clearance and visibility requirements for Visual Flight Rules (VFR) traffic transitioning through the area, potentially restricting access for local ranching, air ambulance, and agricultural flight operations without an adequate safety buffer.

III. PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE AMENDMENT
Instead of full revocation of the airspace as proposed in Paragraph 6005, the FAA should issue a revised NPRM or Final Rule that defers revocation pending a 180-day operational evaluation of RNAV/GPS approach feasibility.

Proposed Alternative Text for 14 CFR Part 71:

Paragraph 6005 Class E Airspace Areas Extending Upward From 700 Feet or More Above the Surface of the Earth
* * * * *
ASW TX E5 Santa Elena, TX [Amended]
Santa Elena, Diamond "O" Ranch Airport, TX
(lat. 26°47'15"N., long. 98°31'05"W.)

That airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface within a 6.5-mile radius of Diamond "O" Ranch Airport, pending completion of the FAA Central Service Center's RNAV/GPS feasibility study for rural emergency and general aviation operations.
* * * * *

IV. CONCLUSION
The FAA should pause the complete revocation of Class E airspace at Santa Elena, TX, perform an operational review of satellite-based approach alternatives, and solicit direct feedback from local emergency medical transport providers before finalizing this rulemaking.
